title: HCI Module 5 — Collaboration and Communication
description: Exam revision: face-to-face communication, conversation mechanisms and rules, text-based communication, group working, media spaces, virtual worlds and dialog design.
endCard: 📘 Collaboration & Communication — revised. You've got this!

scenes.title: Intro

viz.s: Why is face-to-face easy, and text so easy to misread?

lines: Why can two people chat effortlessly face to face, but misunderstand each other over text?
This module is about collaboration and communication.
Face to face communication, conversation, text based communication, group working, and dialog design.

scenes.title: 1. What is face-to-face communication?

items.b: along with intelligence, communication gives us the edge over other animals
communication is a means of transferring knowledge
language is a tool of communication
greatest single discovery in communication before the internet

lines: Along with intelligence, communication is what gives us the edge over other animals.
It is a means of transferring knowledge,
and language is the tool of communication.
Before the internet, the printing press was the greatest single discovery in the field of communication.

scenes.title: 2. Social communication

items.b:
• Face to face
• Over phone
• Voice chat & video conferencing

• Mails (letters)
• Emails
• Instant messenger
• Text messaging

lines: Social communication comes in two kinds.
Verbal communication: face to face, over the phone, voice chat, and video conferencing.
Non-verbal communication: mails, emails, instant messenger, and text messaging.

scenes.title: 3. Conversational mechanisms — greetings
lines: Conversations follow mechanisms and rules. They start with mutual greetings.
A says, hi there. B, hi. C, hi.
A: all right? C: good, how's it going? A: fine, how are you?
C: OK. B: so-so, how's life treating you?
Everyone greets, and every greeting is returned. It's a ritual.

scenes.title: 4. Turn-taking & back-channelling

msgs.t: Um, can we meet a bit later?
Um, can we meet a bit later?

lines: Turn taking is used to coordinate conversation.
A: shall we meet at eight? B: um, can we meet a bit later?
Turns can nest. A: shall we meet at eight? B: wow, look at him! A: yes, what a funny hairdo!
B: um, can we meet a bit later? The original question gets its answer after the side sequence.
Back channelling, like uh-uh, umm, ahh, signals the speaker to continue, and that the listener is following.

scenes.title: 5. Farewells & cues

items.b: “Bye then” · “See you” · “See you later…”
looking at your watch · fidgeting with coat and bags
“Oh dear, must go, look at the time, I'm late…”

lines: Conversations close with farewell rituals: bye then, see you, see you later.
Before that, people send implicit cues, like looking at their watch, or fidgeting with coats and bags.
Or explicit cues: oh dear, must go, look at the time, I'm late.

scenes.title: 6. Sacks et al. (1978) — 3 conversational rules

items.b: current speaker chooses the next speaker by asking an opinion, question or request
another person decides to start speaking
the current speaker continues talking

lines: Sacks and colleagues, in nineteen seventy-eight, described three basic rules of conversation analysis.
Rule one: the current speaker chooses the next speaker, by asking an opinion, a question, or a request.
Rule two: another person decides to start speaking.
Rule three: the current speaker continues talking.
Memory hook: pick, jump in, or keep going.

scenes.title: 7. Breakdowns in conversation
lines: Breakdowns happen when someone says something that is misunderstood.
The speaker repeats with emphasis. A: this one? B: no, I meant that one!
People also use tokens to flag a breakdown: eh? quoi? huh? what?

scenes.title: 8. Text-based communication

items.b: voice only — no facial or gesture cues
asynchronous — long delays between turns
near real-time — turns overlap and interleave
short, abbreviated — tone easily misread
do the same conversational rules apply?
are there more breakdowns?
how do people repair them in each medium?
emoticons, quick follow-ups, clarifying questions

lines: What happens in technology mediated conversations?
Do the same conversational rules apply? Are there more breakdowns?
How do people repair them, over the phone, by email, instant messaging and text messaging?
With fewer cues and more delay, breakdowns rise, so people repair with emoticons, quick follow-ups and clarifying questions.

scenes.title: 9. Group working

nodes.b: support communication where obstacles stop it happening ‘naturally’
let people in physically different locations communicate
carry on communicating as if in the same place

lines: Group working means designing collaborative technologies.
The challenge is to support communication where obstacles prevent it from happening naturally.
The main aim is to let people communicate when they are in physically different locations.
The key issue is letting them carry on communicating as if they were in the same place.
And designers also ask how collaborative technology can help co-located groups communicate.

scenes.title: 10. Communicating across locations

items.b: text-based online worlds — communicate exclusively using text

lines: Tools for communicating across physical locations: emails, video conferencing, and videophones,
computer conferencing, chat rooms, and instant messaging.
And online MUDs and MOOs, multi user dungeons and their object oriented versions, were created to let users communicate exclusively using text.

scenes.title: 11. Dialog design — same game, different dialog

items.b:
> look
Forest path…
> climb tree
You are 10 feet above the ground…
dialog = commands ↔ prose replies

avatars in the scene, chatting:
“does anyone have questions?” · “I'm Larry from Indiana University” · “good to meet you”
dialog = social, many-to-many

lines: Activity: how do the conversations differ for the same game of Zork?
In the text version, you type commands like look, or climb tree, and the game answers in prose.
In the three D world version, avatars stand in the scene and chat, greeting each other, asking questions, introducing themselves.
Same game, but the dialog becomes social. The medium changes the conversation.

scenes.title: 12. 3D virtual worlds

events.b: dress up as an avatar — penguins to real people
avatars explore the world and chat to other avatars
7 million+ players · massively multiplayer online game

lines: Three D virtual worlds. In BowieWorld's rooftop garden, users take part by dressing up as an avatar, including penguins and real people.
Once an avatar has entered a world, it can explore and chat to other avatars.
Massive worlds followed. Second Life, from two thousand three, with over two million users.
And Habbo Hotel, from two thousand, with over seven million players, a massively multiplayer online game.
Think about it: what kinds of conversation take place in these environments?

scenes.title: 13. Media spaces

items.b: combines audio, video and computer systems to “extend the world of desks, chairs, walls and ceilings”
camera + monitor + mic on a desk — an always-on link to a colleague
big wall screen linking two coffee lounges for casual chat across sites

lines: Media spaces combine audio, video and computer systems to extend the world of desks, chairs, walls and ceilings.
Examples: Xerox Media Space, Hydra, Cruiser, and the VideoWindow system.
A typical media space node is a camera, a monitor and a microphone on a desk, linking you to a remote colleague.
The VideoWindow was a large wall display connecting two coffee lounges, so people could chat casually across sites.

scenes.title: 14. Dialog notations, semantics & analysis

items.b: state transition networks, statecharts, Petri nets — dialog as states + arrows
grammars (BNF), production rules — dialog as text rules
what each user action means — the effect it has on the system
check completeness, determinism, consistency and reversibility before building

viz.note: Textbook background — the slides only name these topics

lines: The outline also names dialog design notations. These describe the structure of a dialog between user and system.
Diagrammatic notations draw the dialog, like state transition networks, statecharts, or Petri nets.
Textual notations write it down, like grammars in B N F, or production rules.
Dialog semantics is about what each user action means, the effect it has on the system.
Dialog analysis checks a design for completeness, determinism, consistency and reversibility, before it's built.

scenes.title: Recap

viz.s: Greet · Take turns · Back-channel · Repair · Say goodbye

lines: Quick recap.
Conversations run on greetings, turn taking, back channelling, repair, and farewells. Sacks' three rules: speaker picks, someone jumps in, or the speaker continues.
Technology can stretch this across distance, with email, chat, MUDs, virtual worlds and media spaces. You've got this.
